notes:
I've written up notes on Psalm 48 below. A few things to know first:

- **I hit the search tool's usage limit partway through.** Because of that I read nothing from the Lutheran or Orthodox sites, nothing from catholic.com, and nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching. Those areas are left out, not found to be empty.
- **Some pages were cut short when I fetched them.** Enduring Word stops partway through vv. 12–14, Wesley's notes stop after v. 13, and I only got pieces of Spurgeon's *Treasury of David*.
- **The commentators quote different translations.** Most use the KJV ("sides of the north," "guide even unto death") and Augustine uses the old Latin/Greek text. Where that changes the meaning, I've said so.

**Introduction / title**
- The NET Bible calls this a "Song of Zion." It celebrates Jerusalem as the LORD's home, and says His presence there lifts the city above all others and keeps it safe. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=48
- Gill says some link the psalm to David's defeat of the Philistines (2 Sam 5), others to Jehoshaphat's rescue from Moab and Ammon (2 Chr 20). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/48.htm
- Ellicott says Jerusalem was saved from an alliance of kings by a sudden, unexplained panic. The event looks like Jehoshaphat's victory or the defeat of Sennacherib's army, but which one doesn't matter much. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/48.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary also places it in Jehoshaphat's time. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-48.html
- Spurgeon says the title pairs a "song" (for joy) with a "psalm" (for reverence). https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps048.php

**v. 1**
- Guzik: God is great, greater than all and greatness itself. This "holy mountain" is a contrast to Sinai, which was fenced off from the people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-48/
- Guzik also says the psalmist meant the real, historical Jerusalem but also saw past it to the New Jerusalem (Rev 3:12; 21:2). He says the two meanings support each other. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-48/
- Spurgeon contrasts this with the Ephesian crowd's cry "Great is Diana." He says God's worship should fit His nature, and that only holy people can praise Him fittingly. He applies the city to the church. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps048.php
- Gill applies "Great is the LORD" to Christ and calls Jerusalem a figure of the gospel church. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/48.htm
- Wesley's note is brief: the city is Jerusalem, God's holy mountain. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/psalms-48.html

**v. 2**
- *"Beautiful in loftiness":* Ellicott says the Hebrew word appears only here and probably means "elevation," which suits Jerusalem. It could also just mean "supremely beautiful." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/48.htm
- The NET Bible's reading is that Zion is pleasant to look at because it stands high. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=48
- *"Joy of all the earth":* The NET Bible calls this deliberate exaggeration. Zion is pictured as the capital of the world, which the prophets expected to come true at the end of the age (Isa 2:1–4). https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=48
- Wesley says the line is prophetic, because the gospel was to go out from Zion to all nations. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/psalms-48.html
- Spurgeon says the church is the true joy of the world, even though people despise it. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps048.php
- *"Zaphon / sides of the north":* the older commentators disagree.
  - Spurgeon: either Jerusalem was at the north end of Judah, or this is the part of the city north of Mount Zion. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps048.php
  - Pulpit: the simplest reading is best, that Zion lay north of the temple. Cheyne thought the phrase was a later addition. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-48.html
  - Matthew Henry: Mount Zion sheltered the city from cold north winds. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_048.cfm
  - Ellicott: it could mean the temple's position, or "secret, safe hiding places," a picture of security. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/48.htm
  - Guzik, citing Kidner: Isaiah 14:13 uses "the far north" for God's heavenly throne, so earthly Zion is being described as the heavenly city. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-48/
- *Modern scholarship on Zaphon:* The NET Bible says "peaks of Zaphon" means Mount Zaphon near ancient Ugarit, where Canaanites believed the gods met. By borrowing this, the psalm claims Zion is the real mountain of God, where the LORD rules the nations. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=48
- Utley (bible.org) adds that Zaphon was linked to Baal in the Ugaritic poems. He says the point is that Zion outranks the Canaanite gods' mountain because the LORD is greater than they are. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21547
- *Catholic (Augustine):* the "sides of the north" are the Gentiles. Freed from unbelief, they are joined to the Jewish believers on Christ the cornerstone, so the two "walls" become one city. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801048.htm

**v. 3**
- Ellicott: the stress is on safety that comes from height, so "God…is known as a high and secure tower." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/48.htm
- The NET Bible says the Hebrew is literally "he is known for an elevated place." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=48
- Wesley: God is "known" through long experience. The "palaces" may be the king's palace and the temple, which God protected, and so protected the whole city. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/psalms-48.html
- Spurgeon: we don't worship an unknown God, and we have no refuge but Him. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps048.php
- Augustine works from a different text ("when He shall take her up"). He reads it as grace: without Christ as its foundation the city would fall. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801048.htm

**v. 4**
- *Who were the kings?*
  - Ellicott says it's only a guess. Options include Ammon, Moab and Edom against Jehoshaphat, Sennacherib's vassal kings, or Pekah and Rezin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/48.htm
  - Wesley names Jehoshaphat's enemies or the Assyrian princes (Isa 10:8). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/psalms-48.html
- The NET Bible says the verbs could describe an attack as if it were happening now. Either way, God's victory over Assyria in 701 BC probably inspired the scene. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=48
- Guzik, quoting VanGemeren, says "advanced together" means the kings were confident because they were united. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-48/
- Gill also reads this as the end-times battle of Armageddon, where Christ defeats the gathered kings. That prophetic reading is his own; the other sources keep to history. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/48.htm

**v. 5**
- Several writers think of Caesar's "I came, I saw, I conquered." These kings came, saw, and fled, without a single weapon being drawn in the city. Guzik cites Boice and Maclaren for this. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-48/
- Ellicott makes the same point and notes the Hebrew has no "and" between the verbs, which makes it fast and vivid. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/48.htm
- Spurgeon: they did not conquer, but ran as soon as they saw the LORD was in the city. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps048.php
- The NET Bible says what they saw was the LORD showing Himself as the city's defender (v. 3). https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=48
- Wesley: they only looked at the city and never shot an arrow at it (2 Kgs 19:32). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/psalms-48.html

**v. 6**
- Wesley links their fear to news of Tirhakah's approach and the slaughter of the Assyrian army (2 Kgs 19). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/psalms-48.html
- Spurgeon calls the labor-pain picture a common Eastern way of describing extreme anguish. He says God's proudest enemies will be like trembling women. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/tod/psalms/48.htm
- The NET Bible notes the wording echoes Exodus 15:15. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=48

**v. 7**
- *Real ships or a picture?*
  - Ellicott: Jehoshaphat's wrecked fleet (1 Kgs 22:48) may lie behind the image, but here it is a picture of a land army being scattered. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/48.htm
  - Pulpit: a literal reading doesn't fit, because no fleet was involved. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-48.html
- The NET Bible: "ships of Tarshish" were the biggest ships of their day and stand for mere human strength. The verb tense suggests this is something God regularly does. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=48
- Spurgeon applies it to the church: God breaks false teachings that promise wealth, and the human props the church leans on. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps048.php
- Augustine: Tarshish may be Tarsus or Carthage, and the ships stand for the pride of the nations. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801048.htm

**v. 8**
- Guzik: God keeps His promises in our own day, not just in the past. Quoting Boice, he says what we have heard about we should come to see for ourselves. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-48/
- The NET Bible: having seen God's power themselves, the people could confirm the old stories were not exaggerated. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=48
- Ellicott thinks the poet may have had the Exodus in mind, and that this line is a refrain of the song. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/48.htm
- **Where traditions differ: "God will establish her forever"**
  - Wesley (Methodist) makes it conditional. God would have defended Jerusalem in every age if the city had not forsaken Him and lost His protection. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/psalms-48.html
  - Gill (Baptist) applies it to the church built on Christ the Rock, which the gates of hell cannot defeat. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/48.htm
  - Matthew Henry (Nonconformist) also takes it as the church established forever on a rock (Matt 16:18). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_048.cfm
  - Spurgeon (Baptist) uses Zion's defenses (vv. 12–13) to teach the security of believers and the "final perseverance of the saints." https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps048.php
- *Catholic (Augustine):* the church heard in prophecy and now sees fulfilment in the gospel. Because God founded the city forever, it will not fall, and its unity is set against heretics and schism. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801048.htm

**v. 9**
- Guzik: the focus moves from God's power to His covenant love (*hesed*). He lists the ways the temple showed that love, including meeting with God, sacrifice and prayer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-48/
- Ellicott thinks this verse suggests the psalm was written for worship services. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/48.htm
- Wesley: it was the subject of deep thought during temple worship. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/psalms-48.html
- Augustine's text reads "we have received your mercy in the midst of your people." He takes it to mean that not everyone who receives the sacraments receives God's mercy. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801048.htm

**v. 10**
- The NET Bible: God's "name" means His reputation and character, and His "right hand" means His power in action. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=48
- Ellicott: God's praise lives up to the fame His deeds have earned. His hand is full of justice, not thunderbolts like the pagan god Jove's. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/48.htm
- Spurgeon: God's hand is never empty. Through Jesus He is just to forgive the believer, and He is just to condemn the sinner. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/tod/psalms/48.htm
- Wesley: God is recognized as being who He says He is in His Word. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/psalms-48.html
- Augustine: God's praise is not limited to one region but reaches the ends of the earth. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801048.htm

**v. 11**
- *"Daughters of Judah"* means the towns and villages of Judah. This is the view of Kidner (via Enduring Word), the NET Bible, Ellicott and the Pulpit.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-48/
  - https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=48
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/48.htm
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-48.html
- Spurgeon accepts the towns reading and adds that the women, who suffer most in war, should be gladdest. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/tod/psalms/48.htm
- The "judgments" are God's acts against the enemies in vv. 4–7. The NET Bible, Wesley and the Pulpit say this.
  - https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=48
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/psalms-48.html
- Augustine reads "Judah" as "confession," so the "daughters" are those who confess Christ. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801048.htm

**v. 12**
- Ellicott: the people are invited to inspect the defenses. Unlike a Greek orator praising the men who made Athens strong, the Hebrew poet credits it all to God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/48.htm
- Wesley and the Pulpit: count the towers and find that none have been destroyed.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/psalms-48.html
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-48.html
- Matthew Henry: this may be a victory procession around the walls (compare Neh 12:31). He applies it to the gospel church (Heb 12:22). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_048.cfm
- Spurgeon: the enemies counted the towers in envy and then terror, and we should count them with joy. Christians should know the church better than their account books. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps048.php

**v. 13**
- The NET Bible: the word translated "tour" appears only here and its meaning is uncertain. The towers and walls are visible reminders of God's protection. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=48
- Ellicott: the word means taking the palaces one by one. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/48.htm
- Spurgeon: we have received the truth and must pass it on, learning so that we can teach. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps048.php
- Guzik applies it to telling the next generation how we have experienced God's faithfulness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-48/

**v. 14**
- Guzik: the psalm turns our eyes from the towers to God Himself, the source of the city's glory, who is ours forever and guides us to death. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-48/
- Spurgeon: He is His people's covenant God forever, and there is no other God we would want. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/tod/psalms/48.htm
- *"Even till death"* is debated:
  - Ellicott says the ancient versions and manuscripts show the Hebrew words ('al-mut) are really a musical note, probably moved from the title of the next psalm. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/48.htm
  - The NET Bible says the words make little sense as they stand. It rejects Dahood's suggestion of "for eternity" and prefers a musical note that belongs with Psalm 49's heading. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=48
  - A writer quoted in Spurgeon's *Treasury* (not named in my extract) reads it devotionally as "beyond death." God leads His people over death to resurrection, like crossing the Jordan into Canaan. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/tod/psalms/48.htm
